_comment: Hand-curated notes on places the old city is actually known for, keyed by
the OSM id the extract carries — every key below was verified to exist in
data/anchors/oldcity_places.geojson, so none of these can point at nothing.
This is the one place in the project where a human wrote a fact about the
real world rather than the sim generating one. Everything else the UI shows
is folded from the log. Keep it that way: these are notes on the GEOGRAPHY,
never on the simulated people who happen to be standing in it.
`est` is a year or century as commonly given; where sources disagree the
note says so rather than picking. Devanagari names are the common local
spelling, not a transliteration of the Latin.

way/264276391.note: Founded by a sweet-seller who lost his son to the plague. Bal Gangadhar Tilak turned the private worship of exactly this kind into the public Ganeshotsav a year later, as a way to gather crowds the Raj could not ban. The city's richest temple, and its most visited.

node/2289294092.note: The gramdaivat — the city's own presiding deity, installed by Jijabai when Shivaji was a boy. Pune's Ganesh processions still leave from here first, ahead of every wealthier temple.

node/2358247542.note: The last Peshwa's town house, and the reason this peth looks the way it does: a seven-storey wooden facade of carved teak that survived the fire the Wada itself did not. Used as a college, then a post office, now partly a museum.

way/380363669.note: The temple the market grew around, not the other way about. Its shikhara is visible from four lanes away; everything under it sells bangles, steel vessels and plastic buckets.

node/10172994194.note: The market itself — the densest retail in the old city, and the place a Punekar means when they say they are going shopping.

node/2701228387.note: Older than the Peshwas and older than Shivaji. The goddess is the city's other gramdaivat, and her palanquin has right of way over every other in the Ganpati procession.

way/65486228.note: The city's wholesale vegetable market, built by the British as Reay Market on an octagonal plan with eight wings and a clock tower. Renamed for Jyotirao Phule, who is buried nearby.

way/215535660.note: Built by the Peshwas on the Mutha's bank as a cremation-ground temple, which is why it sits slightly apart from the peth around it.

node/11846700223.note: The three-trunked Ganpati. A small stone temple carrying carvings nothing else in the city has — a rhinoceros, a British soldier, a Persian inscription — and a sealed basement said to hold its founder's samadhi, opened once a year.

way/1044781042.note: One of the surviving wadas — the courtyard house that is the old city's basic unit. Several families around one open square, which is why 1.7 households share a building in this sim and that is not a shortage.

way/365296308.note: Another surviving wada. Of the 450-odd heritage wadas catalogued in Pune, most are gone; the ones left are usually still lived in.

node/5832547676.note: A talim is a neighbourhood wrestling gymnasium, and in the peths it is also a political address: the akhada, the Ganpati mandal and the local strongman have historically been the same institution.

node/5832579354.note: Its Ganpati mandal was founded jointly by Hindu and Muslim families — the only one of the manache Ganpati with that origin, and still described that way in the city.

node/2536024948.note: The elephant Ganpati, named for the stone elephants flanking the door.

way/219767488.note: A peth temple of the kind there are fifty of in this extract: too small to be a landmark, too old and too used to be anything but the centre of its own lane.

node/3836998960.note: Built by Nana Phadnavis's family. The bel trees it was named for are gone; the courtyard is now a car park with a temple in it.

way/885038701.note: The heart of Mominpura, the old city's principal Muslim quarter — one of the four peths in this sim, and the reason its demography is not the same as Kasba's.
